<b>1827</b>Georg Simon Ohm publica que l: 1827Georg Simon Ohm publishes that the current through a conductor is proportional to the voltage across its ends: V = I·R. At first almost nobody paid attention.
<b>1845</b>Gustav Kirchhoff, todavía est: 1845Gustav Kirchhoff, still a student, states the laws of nodes and loops, which divide the current among parallel branches such as the cable and the bird.
<b>1891</b>Se inaugura la primera línea: 1891The first alternating-current high-voltage line opens, from Lauffen to Frankfurt: about 175 km at 15 kV. Raising the voltage makes it possible to carry the same power with less current and fewer losses.

El pájaro y el trozo de cable que hay en: The bird and the piece of cable between its feet are two resistors in parallel through which the line current is divided. It is a problem of Ohm's law and nodes.

We get a voltage of 2.5 mV between the feet and 0.25 µA through the bird.

Las líneas que cruzan el campo llevan la: The lines crossing the countryside carry electricity at 400,000 volts. If you touched one of those cables from the ground, you would die instantly. And yet birds perch on them quite calmly.\n\nDo they have something special? No: what saves them is how they are placed.
pueden pasar por cada cable de una línea: can pass through each cable of a large line.
Por cada cable circula una corriente eno: A huge current flows along each cable, of the order of hundreds of amperes. The cables are made of aluminium with a steel core and are very thick, so their resistance is tiny: about $0.1 "Ω/km"$.\n\nThat is why almost no voltage is lost along the cable: over a kilometre, $ΔV = I R = 500 "A" · 0.1 "Ω" = 50 "V"$, nothing next to 400 kV.
Entre las patas casi no hay tensión: Between the feet there is almost no voltage
between one foot and the other.
The bird's feet are about 5 cm apart. The piece of cable between them has a resistance of $R = 0.1 "Ω/km" · 0.05 "m" = 5 "µΩ"$.\n\nThe potential difference between one foot and the other is Ohm's law applied to that piece: $ΔV = I R = 500 "A" · 5 "µΩ" = 2.5 "mV"$. Less than that of a watch battery.
El pájaro, en paralelo con el cable: The bird, in parallel with the cable
es lo que pasa por el pájaro: el resto s: is what passes through the bird: the rest continues along the cable.
El pájaro y el trozo de cable están en p: The bird and the piece of cable are in parallel between the same two points. The current divides inversely to the resistances: almost all goes through the cable (5 µΩ) and almost nothing through the bird (about 10 kΩ).\n\nThrough the bird passes $I = ΔV/R = (2.5 "mV")/(10 "kΩ") = 0.25 "µA"$, a hundred times less than can be felt.
Lo que cuenta es la diferencia de potenc: What matters is the potential difference
El pájaro está entero al potencial del c: The bird as a whole is at the potential of the cable.
Respecto del suelo, el pájaro está a 400: Relative to the ground, the bird is at 400 kV, just like the cable. But the current does not depend on the potential of one point, but on the difference between two. If the whole bird is at the same potential, nothing passes through it.\n\nOnly on landing is there a small readjustment: the bird charges up to the cable's 400 kV with a tiny, very brief current, the same that a small capacitor would have.
El peligro: tocar dos cosas a la vez: The danger: touching two things at once
pasarían por un ave que tocase el cable: would pass through a bird touching the cable and the tower at the same time.
Si un ave grande, como un águila o una c: If a large bird, such as an eagle or a stork, touches the cable and the tower (which is connected to earth) or two different cables at the same time, the whole line voltage appears between its two contact points.\n\nWith 400 kV and about 10 kΩ, $I = (400 "kV")/(10 "kΩ") = 40 "A"$ would flow: the discharge kills it instantly. That is why on towers in areas with birds the cables are insulated near the supports and perches are placed far from them.
